analysis.one_liner: Raises oil-spill penalties by making polluters pay the higher of two fine formulas.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee in the 112th Congress with no cosponsors, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Water Act so that when a company spills oil or a hazardous substance into U.S. waters, the civil penalty is the higher of the two current formulas: per day of violation or per barrel (or unit) discharged. The same higher-of rule would apply to penalties for gross negligence or willful misconduct. For a large spill, the per-barrel basis could far exceed the per-day basis, meaning bigger fines for big spills. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living near waterways, coastlines, and fishing communities, who bear the costs of oil and chemical spills and would benefit from stronger financial penalties that make companies take spill prevention more seriously. Taxpayers would also be better protected when cleanup costs outrun a company's liability.

how_it_helps.text: For ordinary violations, polluters would owe whichever is higher: up to $25,000 per day of violation or up to $1,000 per barrel (or hazardous-substance unit) discharged.
For gross negligence or willful misconduct, the penalty would also be the higher of the two prescribed formulas, closing a gap that could let a large spill be penalized on the lower basis.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, vessel operators, and chemical facilities that discharge pollutants would pay higher civil penalties—up to $25,000 per day or up to $1,000 per barrel/unit discharged, whichever is higher. Those costs could partly be passed to consumers in energy and product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and chemical companies that spill

drawbacks.text: Higher penalties are ultimately costs for oil and chemical companies, which may be passed through to consumers in prices—though pollution costs themselves are also passed to the public when firms escape them.
The bill received no committee action or debate, so its design was never refined; it changed only two penalty clauses and did not address the broader cleanup-liability framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—stronger financial penalties that make polluters internalize spill costs—is real and cheap to the public, since polluters, not taxpayers, pay. The drawback is that penalties passed to firms can flow through to consumers and could burden small operators more than large ones, and the bill was never debated or amended, so its design was never tested. On balance a modest, honest proposal whose main weakness was lack of support rather than its content.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tester introduced the bill on May 3, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—and the Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without the bill moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies that spill into U.S. waters, because the higher penalty structure was never enacted and civil penalties remained unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no cosponsors joined.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for any vote or recorded partisan split; it had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors.

industries.industry: Oil and gas (vessel and offshore/onshore facility owners and operators)
industries.note: The bill would raise the maximum civil penalties for oil and hazardous-substance spills by requiring the higher of two penalty formulas to apply. It died, so their existing penalty exposure remained unchanged.
Facilities discharging hazardous substances face the same higher-of penalty structure. The bill never advanced, so no change occurred.
